title: Benjamin: Born Through Sorrow, Chosen for Strength
paragraphs:
Benjamin: Born Through Sorrow, Chosen for Strength
The Child Who Entered the World Through Tears—and Became Proof That God Can Rewrite Any Story
There are moments in Scripture that happen so quietly we almost miss them.
No armies clash.
No miracles split seas.
No fire falls from heaven.
Only the painful cries of a dying mother.
A father overwhelmed by grief.
A newborn taking his very first breath.
And in the silence between life and death, a name is spoken that would echo through biblical history for thousands of years.
Benjamin.
Most people know him simply as the youngest son of Jacob.
Few realize he was born inside one of the greatest emotional tragedies recorded in Genesis.
Even fewer understand why his story still speaks to people carrying invisible wounds today.
Because Benjamin's life began exactly where many people think their own future has ended—in unimaginable sorrow.
Perhaps that's your story too.
Maybe your life began in brokenness.
Maybe your childhood carries memories you wish never happened.
Maybe you've buried dreams.
Maybe you've buried people.
Maybe you've wondered if the pain you've inherited has already determined the rest of your life.
Benjamin's story whispers a different answer.
Not because suffering isn't real.
But because Jesus Christ has always been writing redemption into stories long before the cross ever stood on Calvary.
That is the heartbeat of Scripture.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
The account begins in Genesis 35 as Jacob and his family journey toward Ephrath, later known as Bethlehem. Rachel—the beloved wife for whom Jacob had labored fourteen years—goes into difficult labor.
The Hebrew text describes the intensity of the moment with striking realism:

"וַיְהִי בְהַקְשֹׁתָהּ בְּלִדְתָּהּ"
Vayehi behaqshotah belidtah.
Literally,
"And it happened as she suffered severe difficulty in giving birth."

The verb קָשָׁה (qāšāh) means to become hard, severe, difficult, or grievous. Scripture does not romanticize suffering. It tells the truth. Childbirth became devastating. Rachel's strength faded with every contraction.
Then the midwife spoke words that every frightened mother longs to hear:

"אַל־תִּירְאִי"
Al-tir'i.
"Do not fear."
For you have another son.
(Genesis 35:17)
Those words were not empty encouragement.

Throughout Scripture, "Do not fear" repeatedly accompanies God's unfolding purposes. While Rachel would never live to raise Benjamin, the child she delivered would become part of God's covenant story in ways neither she nor Jacob could yet imagine.
But then comes one of the most heartbreaking verses in Genesis.
"As her soul was departing—for she was dying..."
(Genesis 35:18)
The Hebrew expression reads:

"כִּי־מֵתָה"
Ki metah.
"For she was dying."
With what little strength remained, Rachel named her son:

"בֶּן־אוֹנִי"
Ben-'Oni.
Nearly every English Bible translates this as "Son of My Sorrow."
That translation is faithful, but the Hebrew carries even deeper emotional weight.

The word אוֹן ('on) can refer to sorrow, grief, affliction, trouble, or the crushing burden of suffering. Rachel was not simply naming her pain. She was naming the entire emotional atmosphere surrounding the child's birth.
Every time someone would call his name, they would remember the day his mother died.
Imagine growing up carrying a name that constantly reminded everyone of tragedy.
Some people understand that feeling all too well.
Not because of their literal name.
But because labels have followed them their entire lives.
Failure.
Divorced.
Addict.
Abandoned.
Unwanted.
Too broken.
Too sinful.
Not enough.
Many people spend decades believing that the worst thing that happened to them is the truest thing about them.
Benjamin never had to keep that name.
Before the identity of sorrow could define his future, his father intervened.
Genesis 35:18 says:
"But his father called him Benjamin."
The Hebrew reads:

"בִּנְיָמִין"
Binyamin.
The name is traditionally understood as "Son of the Right Hand."
The phrase joins two Hebrew words:
בֵּן (ben) — son.
יָמִין (yamin) — right hand.
In biblical thought, the right hand was not merely a direction. It symbolized honor, authority, favor, strength, protection, inheritance, and victory.
The right hand represented the place of dignity.
The place of trust.
The place of blessing.
Jacob refused to let grief become his son's permanent identity.
The child born through death would instead be remembered through promise.
Centuries later, the symbolism becomes even more breathtaking.
The Messiah Himself would be exalted to the right hand of God.
Psalm 110:1 declares:

"YHWH says to my Lord:
'Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies Your footstool.'"
The Hebrew expression is:

"שֵׁב לִימִינִי"
Shev limini.
"Sit at My right hand."

The New Testament repeatedly identifies Jesus Christ as the fulfillment of this promise. After His death, burial, resurrection, and ascension, He was exalted to the Father's right hand (Acts 2:33; Hebrews 1:3; Hebrews 10:12), the supreme place of authority, glory, and honor.
Benjamin's name does not predict Christ directly, but it beautifully foreshadows a biblical pattern: God delights in transforming what begins in suffering into a testimony of His redeeming grace.

That pattern reaches its climax in Jesus Himself. The cross—Rome's instrument of shame—became the means of salvation. The tomb—humanity's symbol of finality—became the place from which eternal life was proclaimed. What appeared to be history's greatest scandal became the greatest display of divine grace.

Benjamin's life continued to reflect this surprising reversal. He became the beloved youngest son of Jacob, deeply cherished by his father. His presence tested the hearts of Joseph's brothers during the famine, revealing repentance where jealousy had once ruled. From Benjamin's tribe came courageous warriors described as exceptionally skilled with bow and sling (1 Chronicles 8:40; 12:2). Israel's first king, Saul, came from this tribe, reminding us that earthly power without wholehearted obedience cannot secure God's favor. Yet God's redemptive purpose for Benjamin's descendants did not end there.

The apostle Paul—formerly Saul of Tarsus—identified himself as "of the tribe of Benjamin" (Philippians 3:5). Once a persecutor of the church, he encountered the risen Christ and became one of the greatest proclaimers of the Gospel. Once again, God rewrote a story marked by violence into one overflowing with grace.

This is the rhythm of redemption woven throughout Scripture. God does not minimize grief, nor does He deny the reality of suffering. Instead, He enters into it, transforms it, and ultimately points us to the One who bore our deepest sorrow. Isaiah foretold the Messiah as "a man of sorrows" (Isaiah 53:3), and Jesus fulfilled that prophecy by taking our sin, shame, and judgment upon Himself. Through His death and resurrection, those who trust in Him receive a new identity—not defined by their wounds, but by His redeeming love.

Perhaps you have spent years believing that your past has the final word. Perhaps you carry labels spoken over you by others, or names you have silently repeated to yourself. Benjamin's story reminds us that the God of Scripture is not bound by the names that pain gives us. In Christ, there is forgiveness for the guilty, hope for the despairing, healing for the broken, and adoption for all who repent and believe the Gospel. He does not erase your history, but He redeems it for His glory.
If this story has stirred something in your heart, don't keep it to yourself.

I'd also love to hear from you. If this message encouraged you to trust Him more deeply, comment, "Jesus is rewriting my story." Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs today.
One surrendered life can become the beginning of countless redeemed stories.
